newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya sees coffee output at 80,000 tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees coffee output at 80,000 tonnes.

text.p: The Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) on Thursday forecast 1996/97 (October/September) production at 80,000 tonnes and remained upbeat that better weather would lead to a significant production growth in 1997/98.

The forecast was marginally higher than the 78,000 tonnes by board directors at end-March when a drought that had persisted from late November was just ending. It compared with production of 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96 and 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95.

"The rains could mean that production will be higher in 1997/98 but we are still compiling figures," CBK Public Relations Manager Paul Kivila told Reuters. "Farm inputs have increased and farmer income from the crop has improved."
Kivila would not give a specific production forecast.
In the farming community of Kiriani in central Kenya, coffee trees were slightly brown, reflecting the effects of drought.
Farmers there said that drought only made worse crops that had been neglected for years after a global prices slump.

"It is not just drought. Farmers are only starting to tend their trees again. Many (trees) had been neglected for years -- so you could look to better production in future provided world prices remain high," said coffee farmer John Macharia.
Macharia had, in the years of decline in coffee prices, interplanted his farm with beans and maize. He said a neighbour had previously abandoned coffee and switched to dairy farming.
The highlands of central Kenya produce some of Kenya's best grade premium mild arabica coffee.
Prices remained high at the local weekly coffee export auction in Nairobi on Tuesday, gaining by about $40 under heavy buying pressure amid declining good quality.

Premium grade ABs averaged $350 per 50-kg compared to $308 last week while grade AAs averaged $351 from $317. Grade Cs averaged $331 from $284. The Coffee Board of Kenya said it sold 35,697 60-kg bags compared to 35,738 bags sold last week.
Kivila said a campaign mainly by millers to be allowed to sell coffee directly to roasters, bypassing the export auctions, lacked farmer support and appeared to have lost steam.
The board has previously said that wealthy Kenyans, in the name of transparency and competition, were trying to distort the auctions and take control of the industry.

But directors of the Kenya Planters Cooperative Union and Thika Coffee Mills -- who process around 80 percent of Kenya's total production -- spent this week in growing areas west of the Rify Valley trying to drum up support for their campaign.
